description: A process P can allocate a private futex hash via prctl(PR_FUTEX_HASH) and then use sys_futex_requeue() to move another process C's shared-futex waiter onto a bucket in P's private table, rewriting C's futex_q.lock_ptr to point inside P's mm->futex_phash. When P exits, futex_hash_free() calls kvfree(fph) directly with no check for foreign waiters, so C's lock_ptr now points into a freed kmalloc-256 object. When C later unqueues (e.g. via io_uring futex cancel -> futex_unqueue), it performs spin_lock() and atomic_dec() at a predictable offset in the reclaimed slab. By spraying pipe_buffer arrays into that slot, the atomic_dec flips pipe_buffer.flags to set PIPE_BUF_FLAG_CAN_MERGE on a spliced read-only page, yielding a Dirty-Pipe-style arbitrary file overwrite and local root.
location: futex_hash_free() in kernel/futex/core.c; requeue_futex() in kernel/futex/requeue.c
reproduction: 1. Process C submits IORING_OP_FUTEX_WAITV on a shared-mapped futex, parking C's futex_q on the global hash.
2. Process P calls prctl(PR_FUTEX_HASH, PR_FUTEX_HASH_SET_SLOTS, 2), allocating a ~192-byte futex_private_hash in kmalloc-256.
3. P calls sys_futex_requeue with source = C's shared futex and dest = a FUTEX2_PRIVATE futex in P's mm; C's futex_q.lock_ptr is rewritten to &fph->queues[k].lock.
4. P exits; __mmput -> futex_hash_free -> kvfree(fph); C's lock_ptr now dangles into freed kmalloc-256.
5. C sprays pipe_buffer arrays via fcntl(F_SETPIPE_SZ) (4*40=160 bytes -> kmalloc-256); SLUB LIFO reclaims the freed fph slot.

6. C issues io_uring ASYNC_CANCEL + GETEVENTS -> io_futexv_complete -> futex_unqueue; atomic_dec(&hb->waiters) hits offset 64+k*64, i.e. pipe_buffer[1].flags, wrapping 0 -> 0xffffffff and setting PIPE_BUF_FLAG_CAN_MERGE.

7. That pipe_buffer holds a splice()'d page from a read-only file; with CAN_MERGE set, write() to the pipe writes into the file's page-cache page (Dirty Pipe primitive) — overwrite /etc/passwd to add a root account.
technical_details:
Hi --

I've found a use-after-free in the futex private-hash teardown that

gives an unprivileged local user a deterministic write primitive.

sys_futex_requeue() can move a waiter from one process onto another

process's private hash table, and futex_hash_free() frees that table

with a direct kvfree() when the owning process exits, leaving the

foreign waiter's lock_ptr dangling. I've attached a working local

privilege escalation PoC that uses this to get root on stock Ubuntu 26

rc via a Dirty-Pipe-style file overwrite.

As in my prior bugs, I used an LLM to find this, but I validated it

myself and wrote this email. I have relied on an LLM even moreso when

producing the PoC exploit: I have not validated anything in the contents

of this file, except the black-box behavior that it grants me root on

stock Ubuntu 26.

Since commit 80367ad01d93 (2025-05, the private-futex-hash work), a

process can allocate a per-mm hash table for its private futexes via

prctl(PR_FUTEX_HASH, PR_FUTEX_HASH_SET_SLOTS, n). The table lives at

mm->futex_phash and is freed by futex_hash_free() when the mm is

torn down. Waiters queued on private futexes have their

futex_q.lock_ptr pointing at a bucket lock inside this table.

Separately, sys_futex_requeue() (commit 0f4b5f972216, 2023-09) lets a

process atomically move waiters from one futex to another. The two

futexes can have different flags---one FUTEX2_PRIVATE, one not. When

the destination is a private futex in the caller's mm, the waiter's

lock_ptr gets rewritten to point at a bucket in the caller's private

hash table. Nothing checks whether the waiter being moved belongs to

a different process.

The teardown path in kernel/futex/core.c is as follows:

    void futex_hash_free(struct mm_struct *mm)

    {

        struct futex_private_hash *fph;

        free_percpu(mm->futex_ref);

        kvfree(mm->futex_phash_new);

        fph = rcu_dereference_raw(mm->futex_phash);

        if (fph)

            kvfree(fph); // direct free here

    }

The resize path (bd54df5ea7ca) carefully handles replacement with

a different mechanism, some kind of ref-counting. But the exit path

just frees the object. This means a foreign process's futex_q.lock_ptr now

points into freed memory; when that process later unqueues

(via futex_unqueue or io_futexv_complete), it calls spin_lock()

and atomic_dec() on the freed slot.

The requeue path has a comment documenting the assumption this

violates (kernel/futex/requeue.c, requeue_futex()):

    q->lock_ptr = &hb2->lock;

    /*

     * hb1 and hb2 belong to the same futex_hash_bucket_private

     * because if we managed get a reference on hb1 then it can't be

     * replaced. Therefore we avoid put(hb1)+get(hb2) here.

     */

That holds when both futexes are private to the same mm. It does not

hold when requeueing shared->private: hb1 is global, hb2 is in the

caller's private hash, and the waiter's own mm never takes a

reference on it.

I have attached two files; one is a PoC that demonstrates the flaw in a

minimal manner, the other is a PoC that can be used to give root on any

recent linux, including Ubuntu 26 rc with full hardening.

The primitive it makes use of is a spin_lock + atomic_dec at a

predictable offset inside a reclaimed kmalloc-256 slab object.

The attached lpe.c works (I believe!) as follows:

1. Process C submits IORING_OP_FUTEX_WAITV on a shared-mapped futex.

   C's futex_q sits on the global hash. (io_uring's futex

   support is used only as a convenient way to keep a futex_q alive

   across the requeue. It doesn't have a bug to my knowledge.)

2. Process P calls prctl(PR_FUTEX_HASH, PR_FUTEX_HASH_SET_SLOTS, 2).

   struct futex_private_hash has a 64-byte header followed by

   cacheline-aligned buckets, so with 2 buckets the allocation is

   64 + 2*64 = 192 bytes, landing in kmalloc-256.

3. P calls sys_futex_requeue with the source being C's shared futex

   and the destination being a FUTEX2_PRIVATE futex in P's own

   address space. C's futex_q.lock_ptr is rewritten to

   &fph->queues[k].lock where k = jhash2(&addr, ...) & 1.

4. P exits. __mmput calls futex_hash_free which calls kvfree(fph).

   C's lock_ptr dangles into freed kmalloc-256.

5. C sprays with pipe_buffer arrays. It calls fcntl(F_SETPIPE_SZ)

   allocates 4 * sizeof(struct pipe_buffer) = 160 bytes, which also

   lands in kmalloc-256. SLUB LIFO means the spray reclaims the freed

   fph slot.

6. C triggers io_uring ASYNC_CANCEL + GETEVENTS, which runs

   io_futexv_complete -> futex_unqueue. The atomic_dec(&hb->waiters)

   lands at offset 64 + k*64 in the reclaimed slot. For k=0 that's

   offset 64 = pipe_buffer[1].flags. atomic_dec(0) gives 0xffffffff,

   setting every flag bit including PIPE_BUF_FLAG_CAN_MERGE (0x10).

7. That pipe_buffer already holds a splice()'d page from a read-only

   file. With CAN_MERGE set, write() to the pipe appends into the

   file's page-cache page. This is the CVE-2022-0847 Dirty Pipe

   primitive, reached through a different root cause.

I've also attached crasher.c: a minimal trigger. It has just two

processes: P requeues C's waiter then exits, C unqueues. On a kernel

with a diagnostic pr_warn in futex_hash_free, each iteration shows

waiters=1 at the kvfree followed by futex_unqueue reading lock_ptr

inside the freed slot.  KASAN didn't report the spin_lock in my

testing, but I'm not sure why. The pr_warn output demonstrates the

dangling pointer directly.

The attached fix, written by an LLM, walks each bucket before freeing,

dequeues any remaining waiter, and clears its lock_ptr (the documented

"already dequeued" signal that futex_unqueue checks). This prevents

the bug, but I'm way out of my depth on this patch here, so I'm mostly

providing it as helpful information that it stops the crash. I did not write

this patch and do not understand the mechanics well enough to say if

it's worth accepting. I tried my best to write the commit message in a

way that makes sense.

Thanks,

Nicholas

Reproduction: the Ubuntu 26.04 daily cloud image ships a vulnerable

kernel (CONFIG_FUTEX_PRIVATE_HASH is default y, depends only on

FUTEX && !BASE_SMALL && MMU), so no kernel build is needed:

  wget https://cloud-images.ubuntu.com/daily/server/questing/current/questing-server-cloudimg-amd64.img

  cat > user-data <<'EOF'

  #cloud-config

  password: test

  chpasswd: { expire: False }

  ssh_pwauth: True

  EOF

  printf 'instance-id: x\nlocal-hostname: x\n' > meta-data

  genisoimage -output seed.iso -volid cidata -joliet -rock user-data meta-data

  # overlay so the downloaded image stays pristine

  qemu-img create -f qcow2 -F qcow2 \

    -b questing-server-cloudimg-amd64.img disk.qcow2 8G

  qemu-system-x86_64 -enable-kvm -m 2G -smp 4 -nographic \

    -drive file=disk.qcow2,if=virtio \

    -drive file=seed.iso,if=virtio,format=raw \

    -netdev user,id=n0,hostfwd=tcp::2222-:22 -device virtio-net,netdev=n0

  # compile statically on the host (cloud image has no gcc):

  gcc -O2 -static -o lpe lpe.c

  scp -P 2222 lpe ubuntu@localhost:/tmp/       # password 'test'

  # ssh -p 2222 ubuntu@localhost

  sudo useradd -m testuser

  sudo install -o testuser /tmp/lpe /home/testuser/lpe

  sudo -u testuser -i

  id

  # uid=1001(testuser) gid=1001(testuser) groups=1001(testuser)

  su root -c id

  # Password:

  # su: Authentication failure          <- can't become root

  printf 'oot::0:0::/root:/bin/sh\n' > /tmp/p

  ./lpe /etc/passwd 1 /tmp/p

  # [+] SUCCESS on attempt 0

  su root -c id

  # uid=0(root) gid=0(root)             <- now we can

Alternatively, build HEAD with make defconfig and boot your own

rootfs -- defconfig enables CONFIG_FUTEX_PRIVATE_HASH.
title: futex: UAF in private-hash teardown via cross-process sys_futex_requeue leading giving LPE
